imp.voice_memo: Joyce writes as though language itself is the protagonist — restless, associative, always folding back on itself like a wave that never quite breaks the same way twice. The prose moves in tidal rhythms: a sentence will gather momentum through accumulating clauses, each one pressing against the next, and then release into something shockingly plain, almost childlike — 'Yes I said yes I will Yes.' He refuses the tidy summary, the authorial intrusion that explains what a moment means; instead he trusts the moment to mean itself, rendered through the exact texture of a consciousness catching its own drift. His diction is promiscuous in the best sense — Latin liturgy rubs against Dublin slang, Shakespeare against a washerwoman's gossip, the sublime against the bodily and slightly ridiculous. He hears words before he means them: the sound of a phrase, its mouth-feel, its buried etymology, matters as much as its sense. Syntax bends to follow thought rather than grammar, so a sentence may begin in third person and slide, without announcement, into the interior of a mind. He is drawn obsessively to epiphany — the ordinary object or overheard phrase that suddenly carries the whole weight of a life — but he refuses to frame it, to point at it and say: here. The reader must feel the charge without being told to. Time collapses; a smell or a half-remembered song can fold twenty years into a single instant. Underneath the virtuosity there is always tenderness — for the failed, the longing, the embarrassingly human — and it is that tenderness, worn lightly, never announced, that keeps even the most formally daring passages warm to the touch.
